Google Rejected Your Right to Be Forgotten Request: Garante Complaint and Other Options

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

If Google refused your right to be forgotten request, treat the rejection as a first-instance decision, not a final one. In Italy you can resubmit a better-argued request, file a complaint (reclamo) with the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, or bring a claim before the ordinary court, and the choice depends on why Google said no.

Start by reading the reasons in Google's refusal

Google's reply email states the ground for rejection, and that ground dictates the next step. Many refusals are not about the merits at all but about missing information, which a new request can fix within days.

The most frequent reasons fall into a few groups:

  • Insufficient identification – Google could not confirm that the page concerns you, often because the request lacked the exact search terms or your name appears in a different form.
  • Public role – the content relates to your professional life, business activity or a public position you still hold.
  • Recency or seriousness – the events are considered too recent, or too serious, for the public interest to have faded.
  • Journalistic relevance – the page is a news report that Google considers still informative.
  • Accuracy not demonstrated – you claimed the content is false but provided no supporting material.

Identification and evidence problems call for a resubmission. Disagreements about public interest or seriousness are where the Garante or a court become relevant, because they involve a legal balancing that Google has decided against you.

Resubmitting to Google with a stronger case

A second request is worth filing when you can add something new: documents, a narrower list of URLs or arguments mapped to the official criteria. Repeating the same text rarely changes the outcome.

Arguing on the official criteria

European authorities assess delisting with the criteria set out in the EDPB Guidelines 5/2019 on search engine cases, which build on the earlier Article 29 Working Party list. They ask whether you play a role in public life, whether you were a minor, whether the data is accurate, up to date and relevant, whether it involves sensitive or criminal data, and whether its availability causes you disproportionate prejudice. Addressing these points one by one turns a generic plea into a structured argument.

Evidence that tends to change the result

Useful attachments include a judgment or dismissal showing how proceedings ended, proof that you left the role mentioned in the article, and documentation of concrete harm, such as rejected job applications or harassment linked to the result. On accuracy, the Court of Justice clarified in case C-460/20 that you must show the information is manifestly inaccurate, but you do not need a prior court ruling to do so; documents you can reasonably provide are enough.

Filing a complaint with the Garante Privacy

A complaint to the Italian data protection authority asks the Garante to decide whether Google must delist the URLs. The Garante has handled right-to-be-forgotten complaints against Google for years, and its decisions bind the search engine as to the results shown for searches in the EU.

  1. Download the complaint form from the Garante's website and describe the request made to Google, its date and the refusal received.
  2. List every URL concerned and explain, for each one, why the balance now favours your privacy.
  3. Attach Google's reply, your original request, identity documents and the supporting evidence gathered for the resubmission.
  4. Send the complaint by certified email (PEC), ordinary email or registered letter, and keep the delivery receipt.

Under art. 143 of the Codice Privacy, the Garante must decide within nine months, extendable to twelve where the investigation requires it, and must inform you of the status within three months. During the procedure it may ask Google for its position, then order delisting, reject the complaint or partially uphold it. Using the data protection authority for a right to be forgotten dispute costs far less than litigation and does not require a lawyer, although a well-drafted complaint makes a real difference.

Taking the matter to court instead

The alternative to the Garante is a claim before the ordinary tribunal under art. 79 GDPR and art. 152 of the Codice Privacy. Italian law treats the two routes as alternatives: once a court is seized of the same dispute between the same parties, a complaint on the same matter is no longer admissible.

Complaint to the GaranteClaim before the tribunal
RepresentationNot mandatoryLawyer required
CostsLowCourt fees, legal fees, risk of costs
DamagesNot awardedCan be claimed under art. 82 GDPR
Typical useClear delisting disputesComplex cases, claims against the publisher too

A Garante decision is not final either: Google or the complainant can challenge it before the tribunal within thirty days of notification. That possibility is one reason a carefully reasoned complaint matters, since a weak decision in your favour may not survive review.

When a right to be forgotten lawyer is worth involving

Many delisting disputes can be handled without counsel, but some cannot. A lawyer becomes useful when the content concerns criminal proceedings, when the publisher must also be addressed, when you intend to claim compensation, or when the case raises questions of public role that require a careful legal argument.

The strongest cases are built before the first request: an argued file sent to Google is also the backbone of the complaint and, if needed, of the claim.

In practice, Italian cases often combine legal and technical work. While a complaint is pending, the affected person can still reduce the visibility of the disputed pages by building other relevant results, a strategy compared with delisting in our article on removal, deindexing and suppression.

Making a favourable outcome hold

A delisting order covers the URLs it lists, on Google's European versions; following the Court of Justice ruling in C-507/17, it does not automatically extend worldwide. Copies of the same article on new URLs need fresh requests, which is why monitoring your name after a positive decision is part of the job.

The same content may also persist on other search engines, which require their own applications under art. 17 GDPR, and in AI-generated answers that rely on cached sources.
